newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Voters bitter but expect Milosevic victory.
newsitem.headline: Voters bitter but expect Milosevic victory.

text.p: Belgrade voters were bitter and cynical about Yugoslavia's future on Sunday as they queued at polling stations to choose a federal parliament in the country's first elections since a bitter four-year Balkan war ended.
Despite the disenchantment with economic impoverishment and corruption, they still expected Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic's ruling Socialists to win again.
The grim mood at the polling stations contrasted with the optimism among voters, mostly pensioners, interviewed by state television after casting their ballots.

These voters praised Milosevic -- not himself a candidate in these elections -- and his Socialists as the best hope for a better future after five years of political and economic turmoil since the collapse of former Yugoslavia.
But there were few open supporters of the ruling elite in the working class suburb of Kanarevo Brdo whose population has felt the full brunt of unemployment and subsistence-level living standards.
Dragan, a 40-year-old electrician with an unemployed wife and teenage daughter, said: "We will live like this all our lives if these people remain in power.

"While the country was under sanctions and at war, our ministers and bosses got rich. How is this possible in a country under sanctions? With these authorities, there can be no revival of the economy or progress."
A chemical manager said he fared better than most because he had a good job in a stable company but he added:
"My friends and relatives are living miserably. No-one is satisfied. Letting us sell cigarettes and petrol on the black market is simply a way of buying social peace."
Even so, he said, "I believe they (the Socialists and their allies) will win again."
Divorcee Mirjana, 40, sells cigarettes to supplement the 500 dinar ($100) a month salary on which she and her 16-year-old daughter live. The cigarettes bring in another 30 to 50 dinars a day.
"In the West, people live on welfare," she said. "Here we cannot live by honest work. They won't cede power without blood on the streets. But for now the people are afraid."
People's fears focused on the nexus between the Socialist government and the state-controlled industries whose bosses are political appointees.
Many were concerned that privatisation of industry would be used as a means for managers to acquire potentially valuable businesses at knock-down prices.
"My boss, who destroyed our firm, will now buy it," said Dragan. "He will get rich but he will continue to pay the workers 100 German marks a month as he always has."
Across Belgrade in the suburb of Dedinje, home to a mix of middle class and ultra-rich Serbs, Western ambassadors and the political elite including Milosevic, voting was slow during the morning.

A hospital anaesthetist voiced the extent of the credibility problem which confronted the fragile Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties and which worked in favour of the formerly communist Socialists.
To work together, the various Zajedno leaders have had to call a temporary truce over differences which everyone knows still dog the various parties.
The 60-year-old woman acknowledged she was still a communist but added: "The oppositon scares me. If they are at such odds with each other and behave as they do now, how would they behave in power."
